title: Stop resisting
core: All four describe the moment resistance stops and the other side gets its way. They split on the backstory each one assumes: whether a fight ever occurred, how long it lasted, and which party was doing the pressing. They also split on who looks bad afterward — some paint the giver-in as weak, one paints them as having been the harsh one, and one paints nobody badly at all.

words.nuance: The only one where no fight ever happened — the objection stayed inside your head. It measures consent by silence, so it needs a power gap to make sense (a boss, a regime) and it faintly indicts you for not speaking up. Grammar matters: you acquiesce **in** or **to** something.

Demands a prior siege: a standoff, a campaign, months of holding out, then the break. Uniquely, it implies you accept *the other side's terms*, not a compromise — the winner sets the conditions. Applied to a person or institution, it is close to an accusation of cowardice.

The neutral, physical one: the thing **gives** rather than breaks. It can happen instantly, without any prior refusal, and can be a courtesy or a tactic rather than a defeat ("I yield to my colleague"). It also carries a sense none of the others has — to *produce* a return, as a crop or a bond does.

Casts you as the one who was being hard — refusing, punishing, pressing — so the giving way reads as mercy rather than defeat. It is also the only one that takes impersonal subjects: rain, heat, and pain relent. Its negative, relentless, is the far commoner word.

exam_note: The GRE picks between these on backstory, not on strength: sentences signal "held out for months" (relent/capitulate) versus "never objected aloud" (acquiesce) — and it loves testing yield and relent through their adjectives, unyielding and relentless.
